opus-5.5.text:
I think it's a very natural direction, honestly. If you look at how OpenAI has thought about AGI from the beginning, the physical world was always part of the picture. Back when I was there, there was a robotics team, the one that did the Rubik's Cube with the robot hand. That project taught people a lot, but it was also eventually shut down, because at that time the bottleneck wasn't really the algorithm. It was data, hardware, and the cost of iteration. You can run millions of language experiments in the time it takes to collect a small amount of robot data.

What's changed now is the foundation. Large models give you a very strong prior about the world: language, vision, common sense, even some reasoning about physics. So the question is no longer "can we learn everything from scratch with reinforcement learning on a robot," which was basically the old paradigm. Now it's more like, we already have a brain that understands a lot, so how do we connect it to a body and let it learn the last mile through interaction? That's a much more tractable problem, and I think that's why OpenAI and many others are coming back to it.

But I'd also be a bit careful. The physical world is fundamentally different from the digital world in one important way: you can't scale interaction for free. In language and in agents working on computers, you can do huge amounts of RL because environments are cheap and parallel. In robotics, every trial costs time, money, and sometimes breaks things. So whoever wins here probably won't just win on model capability. They'll win on the data flywheel: how you get robots deployed, how you collect useful experience, and how you use simulation and world models to amplify that real data.

So my view is that it's a reasonable bet and probably an inevitable one for any company that's serious about general intelligence. But I don't think it'll look like the ChatGPT moment, where one release suddenly changes everything. It'll be slower, more engineering-heavy, and much more about systems: hardware, data infrastructure, safety, and deployment. The core intelligence may come from the big models, but the physical world will punish you for every detail you get wrong.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it's a very natural step, and honestly a bit inevitable. If you believe the goal is AGI, then intelligence that only lives inside a chat window is incomplete. Humans learn a lot from interacting with the physical world, and a model that never touches it is missing a whole channel of grounding and feedback.

That said, I'd separate two things. One is the question of whether language models can serve as the "brain" for robots. The other is whether OpenAI specifically can build a robotics business. On the first, I'm fairly optimistic. We've already seen that large models give robots a kind of common sense they never had before. You can tell a robot "clean up the table" and it understands what that means, which was unthinkable five years ago. The high-level reasoning and planning problem has been largely transferred to the language model.

The hard part is the low level. Manipulation, contact, dexterity, the fine control loop. This is where data is the bottleneck. On the internet we have trillions of tokens of text, but we don't have trillions of trajectories of a hand grasping a cup. So whoever wants to win in embodied AI has to solve the data flywheel problem, either through massive teleoperation, through simulation, or through some clever way of learning from video. OpenAI's strength is scaling, and if they can find the right data engine, that scaling instinct would transfer well.

My personal view, coming from reinforcement learning, is that the physical world is also where RL truly matters. Language has a lot of structure you can learn passively. The physical world punishes you for mistakes, and you have to learn from interaction. I think the companies that combine strong foundation models with serious RL and real-world data collection will have the edge.

So, in short, I see it as the right direction, with a timeline that's probably longer than the hype suggests. The first products won't be humanoids doing housework. They'll be narrower, more structured tasks where the data is easier to collect. But the trend line is clear, and I'd be surprised if OpenAI stayed out of it.

astra-6.text:
I think robotics is a natural direction for OpenAI, but there’s a big gap between having a model that understands the world through language and images and having a robot that can reliably act in it. You can describe how to pick up a cup, but actually doing it requires dealing with uncertainty: where the cup is, how slippery it is, what happens when your grasp is slightly off.

The exciting possibility is that foundation models can give robots a much broader understanding of tasks. Instead of programming every behavior separately, you could tell a robot what you want, and it could use that understanding to guide its actions. But the physical skills still need to be learned and tested.

So I would watch how OpenAI approaches data collection and learning from interaction. In robotics, you can’t simply assume that more internet data will solve the problem. You need a way to gather experience in the physical world efficiently and safely. If they can build that learning loop, I think the potential is enormous. Getting there will take more than putting a language model inside a robot.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the interesting question is how OpenAI’s capabilities translate into action. In a conversation, a model can give you an answer. In the physical world, it has to perceive what’s happening, choose an action, and respond when the result is different from what it expected.

Robotics could be a natural direction, but strong language and reasoning abilities are only part of the problem. You also need reliable control, physical experience, and a way to learn from failures safely. A robot has to work with uncertainty every time it moves.

So I see a lot of potential, especially if models make robots easier to instruct and more adaptable. But I would judge progress by whether a system can consistently finish useful tasks in unfamiliar environments. That’s a much higher bar than producing an impressive demonstration.
